Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I'm presenting to you a summary of Thematic Panel 1, which was on country-led Sustainable National HIV Responses, Resilient Systems and Financing. I deliver this summary on behalf of my co-chair, Dr. Thiep Alla, Vice Chair of the National AIDS Authority of Cambodia. The first thematic panel, Country-Led Sustainable National HIV Responses, Resilient Systems and Financing, addressed a defining challenge for the global HIV response. The discussion took place against a stark financing reality. Four decades of progress, including millions of lives saved, are now at risk of being reversed. UNAIDS estimates that $21.9 billion will be required annually in low- and middle-income countries through 2030. Yet resources remain far below this benchmark as countries face accelerated donor transitions, growing debt burdens, and competing priorities. Panelists agreed that domestic resource mobilization and international support are not alternatives, but partners in the same effort. The danger is that an accelerated transition that transfers full financial responsibility at a speed not manageable by national institutions and community systems, disrupting prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and community-led services,, and placing a higher burden on those already facing the greatest barriers to care. National experiences demonstrated that domestic ownership is possible through strengthened national budgets and the transition of externally supported initiatives into public systems, contributing to their strength and sustainability, not undermining it. However, transition is not only a financial challenge. It also requires strong institutions that guarantee continuity beyond political cycles, preserve people's trust, and protect people, not merely programs. From the donor perspective, Panelists called not for less cooperation, but for better cooperation, which is predictable, flexible, aligned with national and regional priorities, able to support medium-term planning. Donor investment should strengthen national, local, and community capacities rather than create parallel systems. Speakers also called for action on debt, constrained fiscal space, and fragmentation in the global health architecture. Speakers emphasized that with community-led organizations already under severe pressure, people living with HIV and communities most affected by HIV must participate as structural partners in governance, financing, service design, and accountability, not simply as recipients. Their leadership must be reflected in political commitments and in resources allocated to support their work. Panelists emphasized that integration into resilient primary healthcare systems offers an opportunity for more person-centered care. However, integration must not dilute the HIV response. Dedicated financing must be sustained for prevention, community-led response, and interventions that address stigma, discrimination, punitive laws, and other structural barriers, ensuring that investment translates into equitable access. Concrete pathways include country-led national plans, budgets and accountability frameworks, pooled procurement and local manufacturing, and equitable access to medicines, diagnostics, and innovation, supported by knowledge and technology transfer. Honourable President, ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030 is a milestone, not a destination. The political declaration must commit as to financing the response sustainably and predictably, with communities at its center, before and beyond 2030. I thank you very much, Madam President.

Madam President, Excellencies, colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, it is my great honor to present the chair summary of the salient points of the HLM 2026 Panel 2 on Equitable Access to Science, Technology and Innovation Accelerating HIV Prevention, Testing, Treatment and Care. Panel 2, co-chaired by Mexico and Malawi, discussed the historic opportunities of innovation in today's HIV response and how it can be translated from promise into action. Firstly, there was broad consensus on the power of innovation. Countries highlighted the transformative role innovation played in the past, from single-tablet regimens to the same-day ART initiation. For the current response, the panel highlighted the role of long-acting ARVs in prevention and treatment self-care options, and differentiated service delivery. Countries emphasized the first positive experiences from early implementation of long-acting prevention that removed adherence and access barriers for communities. Secondly, there was also broad consensus that innovation alone does not save lives and change epidemics. Access does. Equity does. And leadership does. The panel called for action to achieve the 40+20 milestones that are needed to achieve the 90% reductions in AIDS-related deaths and new HIV infection. The 40+20 by 2030 sets out a concrete ambition for access and a compact for action. 40 million people living with HIV access treatment, and the three 20s— that's 20 million people using PrEP, including groundbreaking long-acting options, 20 billion people 20 billion condoms for prevention, and 20% of domestic HIV investment allocated to prevention. It was also emphasized that these commitments only matter if they are translated into country milestones and met by financing and action. Thirdly, various constituencies and countries emphasized the role of the communities in ensuring access. Communities themselves explained that all major gains in HIV were hard fought for by communities. Communities organized and pushed for making access real, for bringing down prices and ensuring accountability. Barriers in relation to stigma and discrimination in service delivery need to be overcome. Major gaps remain in harm reduction for past innovation in OAT and overdose prevention, while highlighting the potential of long-acting OAT. Fourth and finally, there is strong need for country leadership in making innovation accessible in a sustainable way. Countries highlighted the importance of strong public health programs for achieving the milestones, data systems, and decentralized services for ensuring access. Implementation capacity needs to keep pace with innovation. There was a particular emphasis to continue ensuring access to prevention, which is at risk of falling behind. Existing prevention options like condoms or sexuality education should not be abandoned, but rather sustained. Countries emphasized that innovation requires predictable and stable resources. A combination of domestic investment and global solidarity in form of international financing. Finally, it was reiterated that innovation can be transformative if people can access it, trust it, and use it. The session ended with a call for all countries and all sectors to come together as fast as possible, as long as it takes, to build impact and seize this historic opportunity to change the trajectory of the epidemic. Thank you, Madam President.

Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I deliver this summary on behalf of my co-chair, His Excellency Dr. Bertrand Sinal, Minister of Public Health and population of Haiti. The third thematic panel, Community Leadership at the Center: Driving an Inclusive and Sustainable HIV Response, reaffirmed that community leadership has been indispensable to progress over more than four decades. The discussion took place amid funding reductions, shrinking civic space, punitive laws, anti-rights movements, and humanitarian emergencies. These pressures disproportionately affect people living with HIV, key populations including gay men and other men who have sex with men, sex workers, transgender people, people who inject drugs, and people in prisons and other closed settings. Young people, women and girls in all their diversity, and other affected communities facing exclusion. Communities build trust, connect people to services, generate evidence, and hold systems accountable. In fragile and humanitarian settings, they often sustain access when formal systems cannot. Meaningful participation must go beyond consultation. Communities need decision-making power over policies, budgets, services, and accountability. The panel called for investment in youth-led responses and meaningful roles in governance and advocacy. Women and girls must help define, design, and monitor integrated services with the resources and protection needed to lead. This requires flexible and predictable funding that reaches community-led organizations, including through domestic financing and social contracting. The panel was clear that enabling legal and civic environments are essential. Criminalization, stigma, and discrimination deter people from accessing prevention, testing, treatment, and care, while restrictions on civic space constrain organizations that deliver services and hold institutions accountable. Speakers called for punitive and discriminatory laws and policies to be reformed, human rights and civic space to be protected, and communities to organize and operate safely. The panel also emphasized that integration cannot simply mean combining services. Communities must shape approaches that respond to the whole person across HIV, sexual and reproductive health, gender-based violence, mental health, non-communicable diseases, and primary health care. Tailored community-led services must be preserved while disaggregated and community-generated data are needed to reveal who is being missed. Madam President, the political declaration must secure community leadership and practice. The 1995, '95, '95 targets cannot be achieved without progress on the 30, 80, 60 community-led response targets and the 10-10-10 societal enabler targets. So recognition must translate into measurable commitments on participation, financing, enabling environments, monitoring, and accountability. Communities already lead. The political declaration must ensure that they have the rights, protection, and resources to lead the HIV response towards 2030 and sustain progress beyond it. I thank you, Madam President.

Thank you, Madam President. President, Excellencies, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the European Union and its member states. We have tabled Amendment 80 to include and gender-based before violence in paragraph 33 of the 2026 Political Declaration. This amendment is a necessary reflection of longstanding internationally agreed language that ensures comprehensive protection for all individuals affected by violence rooted in gender inequality, which includes, but is not limited to sexual violence. The term sexual and gender-based violence is firmly established in United Nations frameworks, including the Pact for the Future, the 2021 Political Declaration on HIV and AIDS, and the CSW agreed conclusions. Its inclusion in this paragraph maintains critical consistency with global commitments while acknowledging that Gender-based violence extends beyond sexual violence, all of which disproportionately affect women and girls, particularly in humanitarian crisis conflicts and climate-related disasters. This aligns with the Global AIDS Strategy 2026-2031, which must guide our response. Omitting gender-based would dangerously narrow the scope of protection, excluding forms of violence that heighten HIV vulnerability and undermine progress toward gender equality. We emphasize that this amendment strengthens the Declaration by upholding inclusive rights-based language. We must not weaken our collective resolve to address all dimensions of violence that perpetuate inequality and endanger lives. The European Union kindly calls on all member states to support this amendment. In addition, we have also tabled Amendment L81 to include key populations in paragraphs 75 and of the 2026 Political Declaration. This inclusion is not only justified by essential, as its absence creates a critical gap in the declaration's alignment with global HIV commitments and represents a setback in the global fight to end AIDS by 2030. The 10-10-10 targets central to ending AIDS as a public health threat can simply not be effectively achieved without explicit recognition of key and vulnerable populations and without tailored rights-affirming interventions for and led by these communities. Their inclusion renders these targets consistent with Global AIDS Strategy 2026-2031, which must guide our collective response. Key populations face disproportionate stigma, discrimination, and violence barriers that severely hinder access to life-saving HIV services. Global evidence demonstrates that these groups face HIV prevalence rates up to 25 times higher than the general population. Yet they continue to encounter barriers in assessing prevention, testing, diagnostic, and treatment services. The European Union calls on all member states to uphold an evidence-based, inclusive, and rights-based HIV response and restore key populations to ensure no one is left behind in the fight against AIDS, HIV/AIDS, with a particular focus on where there will be the most impact. We respectfully ask for these two amendments to be considered separately. Thank you.

We dissociate from any references to targets or objectives that are not aligned with the Global AIDS Strategy. Second, we have to continue to dissociate from uncaveated references technology transfer in the text. We stress that the technology transfer can only be undertaken on a voluntary basis and on mutually agreed terms. This is essential to securing the most adequate and efficient response to future pandemics. Similarly, we also have to dissociate from paragraph 86. The European Union and its member states can only recognize references to to the World Trade Organization Doha Declaration on the TRIPS Agreement and public health that are comprehensive and fully aligned to its text. Third, the UN and its member states also have to dissociate from paragraph 41, which is not the exact verbatim reference of the Pact for the Future on unilateral economic measures that was carefully negotiated and agreed in an overall context of balance. President, Excellencies, while the text before us today falls short in many places, our resolve does not. The European Union is fully and unreservedly committed to the overarching objective of the political declaration, which is to tackle HIV/AIDS as a public health threat and support people living with it at risk of or affected by HIV/AIDS, with a particular focus on key populations and with the support of civil society and community-led organizations. To those listening today who are living with HIV or who have lost loved ones to this scourge, we see you, we hear you, and we will keep fighting with you and for you. Until this disease is no longer a threat to anyone, anywhere, leaving no one behind. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cyprus on behalf of the European Union. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cuba, followed by El Salvador and Nicaragua.

Muchas gracias.

Thank you very much, Madam President. Cuba reaffirms its steadfast commitment to the promotion and protection of the right to health, recognized as a fundamental human right. Despite the complex economic circumstances that our country faces, we continue to guarantee universal, free, and equitable access to health services, including prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and comprehensive care for persons living with HIV. For decades, Cuba has developed a comprehensive response to HIV/AIDS through education, prevention, maternal infant care, and free access to antiretroviral drugs. These efforts have allowed us to reach internationally renowned results and show our political will to not leave anyone behind. We particularly value the inclusion in this political Declaration of a paragraph reiterating the appeal to member states to refrain from implementing unilateral coercive measures, which are a violation of the Charter. These particularly affect countries such as Cuba and affect our development and ability to address diseases such as HIV. The progress made by our country in this area are seriously threatened by the economic, commercial, and financial blockade imposed by the U.S. government. This policy directly affects the national health system, our ability to acquire equipment, technologies, and other essential inputs, including medicines. The situation is even worse due to the tightening of unilateral coercive measures over the last few years, including through the intensified fuel surge— siege that we've seen this year. Restricted access to fuel has generated enormous difficulties for the operation of laboratories, hospitals, cold chains, health transport systems, and other essential services for our population. Those living with HIV are particularly affected by the consequences of these measures. The steps that need to be taken to carry— to ensure diagnosis, to procure equipment, as well as the financial side of the blockade, step up the costs and hamper timely access to essential resources to guarantee continued treatment and quality care. No country should be prevented from acquiring health technology, fuel, or medicines to maintain its basic healthcare. Health should not be used as an instrument for political pressure. Cuba will continue to work to strengthen its HIV response and to guarantee the well-being of its entire population. We reiterate our commitment to international cooperation, solidarity, and multilateralism. As essential tools to address the global health challenges. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cuba. I now give the floor to El Salvador.

Muchas gracias.

Thank you very much, President. El Salvador would like to express its thanks to Ambassador Charles Massoff from Botsuana and David Basqerze from Georgia for the transparent, inclusive, and balanced and professional way in which they led the negotiations on the political declaration that we have just adopted. Their leadership enabled us to reach a text that reflects the international commitment that is needed to strengthen the global response to HIV/AIDS and to move towards the goal of bringing an end to this epidemic as a threat to public health. El Salvador reaffirms its steadfast commitment to the implementation of this political declaration and to complying with the agreed targets to reduce new infections, expand access to treatment and comprehensive healthcare, as well as to strengthen international cooperation in this area. This position is based on our interpretation and national position regarding the content of that paragraph. I thank the distinguished representative of El Salvador. I now give the floor to Nicaragua.

Thank you, President. We particularly welcome the recognition of their impact on access to medicines, technologies, and essential services, as well as the ability of countries to implement effective responses to HIV/AIDS. For Nicaragua, the recognition of this reality within the political declaration represents an important element that contributes to reflecting in a balanced manner the challenges faced by many countries in implementing their commitments in public health and sustainable development. Furthermore, it contributes to raising the profile of and corroborating the adverse impact of unilateral coercive measures on states' abilities to guarantee timely, equitable access to services, technologies, and treatments in the health system, making it easier to address this issue in global debates on Health and Development, we reiterate our commitment to international cooperation, solidarity among peoples, to strengthening national sustainable responses to bring an end to HIV/AIDS as a global public health threat. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Nicaragua. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Uganda. Mr.

President, I deliver this statement on behalf of the Republic of Uganda to explain our position on the political declaration on HIV and AIDS on the theme United to End AIDS. At the outset, we would like to thank the two co-facilitators, the permanent representatives of Botsuana and Georgia for their tireless efforts in facilitating consultations on this political declaration at a time of urgent need for the concerted work of multilateralism guided by the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Uganda voted for this declaration in spite of significant shortcomings in the text. Under the Presidential Fast Track Initiative to End AIDS as a Public Health Threat by 2030 and our National HIV/AIDS Strategic Plan, under the Presidential Fast Track Initiative to End AIDS as a Public Health Threat by 2030 and our National HIV/AIDS Strategic Plan, Uganda has made significant progress efforts in reducing new HIV infections and expanding access to prevention, treatment, and care services. In this regard, we stress the sovereign rights of member states as set forth in the Charter of the United Nations to implement their commitments and obligations in line with the national laws and priorities, while respecting the religious and cultural values of the— these societies. We would also like to stress that in this and related communications and resolutions, it is important to highlight the guiding role of the family and to take into consideration the differing national approaches and laws on age-related matters, particularly with regard to sexual and reproductive health issues, parental and guardian involvement, and comprehensive education on matters related to reproductive health. We further stress that each country retains the sovereign right to define the populations most affected by the epidemic according to their own national epidemiological and legal context and to determine accordance with its national legislation the legal and policy framework most appropriate to its African countries' HIV response. In conclusion, we believe that the political declaration we have adopted today needs further work and follow-up to achieve an increased level of determination in addressing the challenges that still exist. We request that this statement be reflected in the official record of this meeting. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished Representative of Uganda. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Switzerland.

Madame President, Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, Switzerland voted in favor of the text of the political declaration and takes the opportunity to thank the co-facilitator for the commitment. We welcome the improvement to the text, in particular the inclusion of sexual and reproductive health services in paragraph 11 and the reference to gender and racial inequalities in paragraph 41. Switzerland also welcomes the inclusion of key populations in the amended paragraph 75, as this better highlights their specific needs and the fight against stigma and discrimination. Without this addition, this aspect would have— would be weakened, and human rights-related barriers will no longer be fully taken into account. With regard to paragraph 85, we emphasize that there are limits anchored in relevant international law to publicizing information such as production costs. Paragraph 85 raises concern regarding the protection of trade secrets and more fundamentally what the role of state authorities can be in relation to private sector actors. Therefore, Switzerland does not support the first part of paragraph 85. With regard to technology transfer, like others, Switzerland dissociates itself from paragraphs 80, 82, 84, and 87. We would like to recall that technology transfer should always be on mutually agreed terms. With regard to paragraph 87, we also emphasize that our concerns regarding alternative mechanisms to remunerate innovation have not been taken into account., which constitutes a second reason why Switzerland dissociates itself from paragraph 87. This said, Switzerland will continue to engage constructively on this issue, and thank you for your attention. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Switzerland. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Belarus.

Thank you, sir. Mr. President, the Republic of Belarus consistently supports international efforts to combat HIV/AIDS, and we view providing for the health of people as one of the key priorities within our state social policy. In Belarus, we are implementing a comprehensive approach to prevention, diagnostic, and treatment diagnosis and treatment for HIV infection on the basis of the principle of universal access to medical assistance, social support, and taking national specificities on board. We note the significance and importance of cooperation with specialized UN system agencies, including UNAIDS, UNDP, and UNICEF. We view this high-level meeting as an important opportunity for the consolidation of international efforts and for the crafting of practical solutions to achieve global goals in countering HIV/AIDS. At the same time, it behooves us to note the fact that the negotiations process has not allowed us to fully take into account the concerns of a number of member states. Belarus values the fact that the draft declaration has provisions retained which contain— which reflect the importance of the role of the family in countering HIV, in treatment, care, and support of people living with HIV or affected by this issue. It is important that the text reflects the role of the family as well as cultural, moral, and religious factors in countering the HIV/AIDS epidemic. At the same time, Belarus continues to have serious questions which are related to certain provisions of the draft document with terminology that is and does not reflect a universal acknowledgement and understanding among member states and allows for selective interpretation. We are talking, inter alia, about language linked to sexual and gender-based violence and multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination. We would also like to note the provisions of paragraph 63 in the operative part of the document. Belarus is not in a position to embrace the interpretation of this provision, which can be viewed as extending support for a notion of comprehensive sexual education. Matters pertaining to the content of educational programs need to be dealt with by states independently in a manner that reflects their national legislation, cultural moral and, and other values and ethical values, as well as in a manner that respects the main role of parents and legal guardians in rearing children. We underscore the inadmissibility of states imposing unilateral coercive measures which fly in the face of international law and the Charter of the UN, and they have an adverse impact on the provision of access to persons in need, their access to medicines and medical technologies in countering HIV/AIDS, we also believe that by no means does the Declaration grant the right for intervention in matters which, in essence, fall within the purview of legislation of states. And through its implementation, states should not have approaches and practices imposed upon them, approaches and practices that diverge from their historical, cultural, and religious traditions, as well as social models. In light of the above, the Republic of Belarus stands ready to conscientiously participate in implementation of the Declaration. Thank you for your attention.
I thank the distinguished representative of Belarus. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Turkiye.

Thank you, Mr. President. Türkiye welcomes the adoption of the 2026 Political Declaration on HIV/AIDS, which provides important guidance for accelerating our collective efforts to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030. Türkiye extends its appreciation to the co-facilitators for their dedicated efforts and their commitment to guiding an inclusive and transparent negotiation process. Turkey has actively and constructively participated throughout the negotiations, recognizing the urgency of sustaining global momentum at this critical juncture and contributing to a declaration that supports accelerated progress in the HIV/AIDS response. We attach great importance to the global fight against HIV/AIDS. The declaration rightly underscores the urgency of the moment. The continued rise in new infections in several regions, the 8.8 million people still without access to treatment, and the persistent inequalities that hinder progress. Turkey implements a wide range of programs aimed at the prevention and control of HIV/AIDS. Consistent with the UNAIDS 95-95-95 global targets and a human rights-based approach, we have developed a national HIV/AIDS control program for 2025-2030. 2030. This program provides strategic guidance for our national response and aims to address the risk factors that contribute to the spread of HIV, ensure that every individual has equitable access to diagnosis, treatment, care, and support, and strengthen public health. Our program also emphasizes that reducing stigma, ensuring confidentiality, and safeguarding equal access to diagnosis, treatment, care, and support are essential to both public health and the well-being of people living with HIV. Türkiye remains committed to advancing an environment in which individuals can seek services without fear of stigma or prejudice, consistent with the Declaration's call to end inequalities and uphold human rights. Türkiye also values the Declaration's reaffirmation in paragraph 13 of the important role played by families, communities, and cultural, ethical, and religious factors in HIV prevention, treatment, care, and support. We consider this recognition essential for ensuring that national responses remain context-appropriate and grounded in approaches that are meaningful and effective for our societies. Mr. President, in this regard, Türkiye wishes to clarify its interpretive understanding for the record. As Türkiye strongly advocates the international efforts in fighting HIV/AIDS, we supported the declaration despite our reservations to certain language in the Turkey would like to register that it treats gender and related concepts and terminology in accordance with its national legislation, which recognizes equality between men and women. This position is consistent with the Declaration's reaffirmation of the sovereign rights of member states as enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations and of the need to implement the commitments and pledges contained therein in accordance with national laws, national development priorities, and international human rights. Turkey will remain a committed partner in advancing the implementation of the Declaration and in promoting equitable, human-centered, and evidence-based approaches to end AIDS by 2030. Mr. President, we also wish to place on record our interpretative understanding regarding the terms indigenous peoples and local communities as referenced in the Political Declaration. Türkiye declares that that there does not exist any group of people in its territory which could be considered as indigenous peoples and believes that the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples refers to the exercise of self-determination in line with the UN Charter obligations regarding non-interference in the sovereignty, integrity, and political unity of states. The relevant paragraphs in the declaration should be interpreted as applicable only to the stand that they are consistent with and implementable under national legislation. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Türkiye. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Burundi.

Merci beaucoup. Thank you, Mr. President. My delegation associates itself fully with the statement delivered on behalf of the African Group. And we fully align ourselves with the state, with the concerns that were voiced and the profound disappointment that was expressed during that statement. We remain resolutely engaged and committed to combating HIV/AIDS, and we recognize the importance of international cooperation to end this pandemic as a threat to global health by 2030. Nevertheless, we were not in a position to support this political declaration. Our position emanates from the fact that the text which should have purely been focused on public health was significantly politicized with the introduction of concepts and approaches which are not subject to international consensus and which are incompatible with our national legislation, our cultural values, our moral principles, as well as our religious convictions. Any initiatives to combat HIV/AIDS need to fully respect the sovereign right of states and be in line with national priorities, their legal, cultural, and religious realities. My delegation rejects in particular the multiple references to the alleged key populations with sexual and gender identity, comprehensive sexual education, as well as the sexual and reproductive health centers and reproductive rights. These are highly controversial notions. They do not reflect the agreement of all member states. We appreciate the fact that the declaration reflects the importance of the family and their important role in prevention, treatment, and care for HIV. And yet we regret the fact that the same document fails to advance nor protect parental consent and does not recognize the key role and the fundamental authority of parents in bringing up and providing moral support and guidance for children on such sensitive matters such as sexuality. We are also concerned by the provisions calling for revision or reform of national legal frameworks, specifically the references to laws related to consent age and other consent-related matters. These are liable to undermine the sovereign prerogative of states and their legislation accordance with national priorities and to undermine the role of parents in upbringing up their children. This can undermine parents' rights and run counter to legal guarantees for minors. We firmly believe that parents are the primary educators for their children, and their rights to education, their responsibility and authority need to be fully respected and upheld. Furthermore, and this is important in particular, we firmly reject and vehemently paragraph 77, which is a direct attack against the institution of marriage and one of its most basic principles, namely mutual consent between the spouses. By seeking to, to, to, to set aside one spouse on sensitive issues. This undermines trust, shared responsibility, and the values upon which families are based. It is unacceptable for international texts to promote approaches which deliberately erode the foundation of family and the family unit, which is universally recognized as the national and foundational unit of society. For all of the above, We— reasons we disassociate ourselves from the political declaration. Our inability to support this declaration should not be interpreted as a lack of commitment to combating HIV/AIDS. Quite the contrary. Burundi continues to remain fully committed to advancing preventive treatment, care services, and support for all persons affected by HIV/AIDS while preserving the values which underpin our society, specifically the central role of the family as a natural foundational unit. Of society. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Burundi. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Paraguay.

Gracias.

Thank you, President. The fight against HIV/AIDS is a priority for the Republic of Paraguay. Over the last few years, the country has strengthened its national response through expanding prevention, diagnosis, and treatment services, making specific progress in ensuring comprehensive care for those living with HIV, and in reducing maternal-infant transmission. Paraguay reaffirms the importance of maintaining international commitment to speed up the response to HIV and to move towards the elimination of AIDS as a threat to public health. However, Following a careful review of the text of the political declaration this year, United to Bring an End to HIV/AIDS, we've decided to abstain on the adoption. This abstention is in line with our understanding of the terminology, which is not in line with constitutional frameworks and— of each country. In particular, Paraguay understands that the reference to sexual and reproductive health and to concepts related to gender should be interpreted in line with relevant legislation and national frameworks. Likewise, the references to the SDGs and the Agenda 2030, including— should include their voluntary and non-legally binding nature. A longer version of this statement will be uploaded to e-delegates, and we suggest that it be included as a working document. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Paraguay. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mexico.

Thank you very much, President. Mexico thanks the co-facilitators, the permanent representatives of Botswana and Georgia, as well as UNAIDS, and all delegations for their work and commitment throughout this negotiation process. My delegation decided to support the adoption of this political declaration, voting in favor, in recognition of the importance of renewing the political commitment of the international community to bring an end to AIDS as a threat to public health by 2030. Mexico believes that the response to HIV should continue to be guided by the best available scientific evidence, human rights, gender equality, equity and a people-centered approach. Throughout the negotiations, we promoted a text fully reflecting these principles and responding to the challenges that continue to fuel the epidemic in various regions and population groups. In this regard, we regret that the final text did not fully preserve some elements that we deem fundamental, particularly stronger references to human rights, the elimination of stigma and discrimination, the role of community-led organizations, and the need to guarantee inclusive responses for people and groups that face greater barriers to access prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care services. In addition, my delegation would have appreciated having more robust references on health and sexual and reproductive rights, as well as comprehensive sexuality education. The value of such education in HIV prevention, particularly among adolescents and young people is amply backed up by, by scientific evidence and by prior agreed commitments at the international level. Nonetheless, despite these considerations, we believe that the declaration does contain important commitments to strengthen the global HIV response, including access to health services, strengthening health systems, ensuring sustainable financing, research, innovation, access to technologies for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. Mexico reiterates that innovation can only fully keep its promise when its benefits reach everyone. Scientific and technological progress should go hand in hand with resolute efforts to guarantee equitable, affordable, and timely access, particularly for those in situations of vulnerability. The experience gained over more than 4 decades of the HIV response also shows that communities are essential actors to ensure sustainable results. Without their meaningful participation, their leadership and experience, it will not be possible to meet the goals that we're setting today. Therefore, Mexico reaffirms its commitment to the effective implementation of this political declaration and to the strengthening of an HIV response based on evidence, human rights, international solidarity, and the active participation of communities and those most affected by this disease. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Mexico. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malawi to speak on behalf of the African Group.

Chairperson, Excellencies, and all distinguished delegates. On behalf of the African Group, allow me, Chairperson, to convey the African Group's appreciation for the support for the amendment table today. We are convinced that with the adopted amendment, the text is improved and reflects the realities needed on the ground. Furthermore, the international community has once again demonstrated its commitment to the HIV and AIDS response, thereby assisting developing countries, including Africa, in the fight against HIV and AIDS through prevention, treatment, care, and innovative cures. We therefore encourage the international community to continue with concrete actions in ending HIV and AIDS as a public health threat by 2030, which is key to leaving no one behind. I thank you for your attention.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malawi. I now give the floor I now hand over to the distinguished representative of Australia to speak on behalf of CANZ.

Thank you, President. I have the honor to speak on behalf of Canada, New Zealand, and my own country, Australia. At the outset, we want to thank Botswana and Georgia for co-facilitating this process. CANZ welcomes the adoption of this political declaration. We strongly support its emphasis on prevention, equitable access to treatment and care, and recognition that effective responses must be grounded in evidence-based, human rights-based approaches, including gender equality, and informed by the meaningful engagement of affected communities. We welcome the declaration's reaffirmation of the importance of sexual and reproductive health services in the HIV response. We underscore the centrality of community-led responses and the need to maintain a strong and sustained focus on key populations who continue to be disproportionately affected and face significant barriers to services. We welcome the additions made today to paragraph 75. While Cairns can engage constructively throughout this process, I want to underline that the final declaration does not fully reflect our priorities in a number of areas. In particular, we emphasize the importance of comprehensive rights-based approaches, including clear recognition of key populations and addressing structural barriers such as stigma, discrimination, and punitive or restrictive laws. Sexual and reproductive health and rights are also integral, ensuring access to quality services and age-appropriate comprehensive sexuality education. We also note with serious concern the last-minute changes to language in paragraphs 80, 82, and 84 on access to medicines and technology transfer. The removal of "on mutually agreed terms" is a departure from formulations agreed in many other recent UN declarations. Our voting in favor of the political declaration today should not be interpreted as agreement with every element of the text. Rather, it reflects our shared recognition of the urgency of this moment and the importance of working collectively to maintain ambition and accelerate progress towards our shared goal of ending HIV/AIDS by 2030. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Australia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of United Kingdom.

Thank you, President. The United Kingdom would like to thank the permanent representatives of Botswana and Georgia for their work in facilitating this process, especially on an expedited basis. The United Kingdom is committed, committed to ending AIDS and welcomes this opportunity to reiterate the essential need for a global HIV response that is inclusive, human rights and evidence-based, and driven by communities, ensuring the full and meaningful engagement of key populations. We voted in favor of the political declaration and welcome its clear targets on ending AIDS by 2030. We also— we are also pleased to see the focus on domestic financing, health systems integration, and innovation to build a more sustainable, future-based approach to the global HIV response. However, there are aspects of the text where we feel strongly that the political declaration should have gone further on. This is why we supported the amendments to reinstate the language on gender-based gender-based violence in paragraph 35. Gender-based violence reflects a broader scope than sexual violence, capturing how sexual, physical, and mental harms increase— increases vulnerability to HIV, especially in times of crisis. Likewise, we also supported the amendments to reinsert key populations in paragraphs 73A and B. As its omission is inconsistent with the Global AIDS Strategy and the 2021 Political Declaration and fails to recognize the heightened stigma, discrimination, violence, and HIV vulnerability faced by these groups, including women and girls. It also risks compromising effective implementation of the commitments in this Political Declaration. With respect to paragraphs 80, 82, and 84, we wish to stress that the inclusion of 'on voluntary and mutually agreed terms' is essential when referring to technology and knowledge transfer. It is imperative that such transfers be on voluntary and mutually agreed terms in order to maximize the chances of successful and long-lasting technology transfer taking place and reducing the possibility of unequal and unfavorable terms so that they are mutually beneficial to all parties, including those from low- and middle-income countries. We regret that an amendment was tabled to delete the language on mutually agreed terms in paragraphs 80, 82, and 84, and we would like to disassociate from these paragraphs. We would also like to express serious concern on several other issues. We would like to disassociate from language referencing healthy lifestyles, risk-taking behavior, and culturally and contextually relevant interventions noted in paragraph 34. This shifts emphasis away from the structural and rights-based drivers of HIV risk towards individual behavior change. And dilutes established commitments to targeted evidence-based interventions for key populations. We would also like to express strong concern with paragraph 77, which has weakened agreed commitments on spousal consent and other structural barriers. The United Kingdom, however, remains committed to our collective efforts to end HIV/AIDS as a public health threat and looks forward to working with with member states, civil society, and all partners to deliver on this commitment. We request that this statement be reflected in the record of this meeting. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of United Kingdom. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Republic of Tanzania.

Mr. President, I commend the Permanent Representative of Botswana in Georgia for facilitating the negotiation for this political declaration to this fruitful outcome. However, Tanzania regrets that despite a shared understanding that the 2021 political declaration on HIV and AIDS would serve as the baseline for the renewed commitment and that collectively— collective efforts would seek to preserve and build upon previous agreed commitments, key development-oriented elements which are critical to ending HIV as a public threat, have been significantly weakened in the final text. For Tanzania, ending HIV/AIDS requires a balanced approach that gives equal weight to prevention, treatment, care, health system strengthening, financing, research and innovation, community engagement, socioeconomic development, and the human rights dimension of the response. We believe sustainable progress cannot be achieved through a narrow focus on any single pillar. Mr. President, Tanzania dissociates itself from interpretation of paragraph 75 that may undermine the principle of responsibility, transparency, and accountability in HIV prevention efforts. While emphasizing the reforms of law related to HIV nondisclosure, exposure, and transmission, the paragraph does not adequately recognize personal responsibility, informed decision-making, the protection of vulnerable persons, and the sovereign rights of states to determine appropriate public health measures in accordance with national circumstances. We also disassociate ourselves from paragraph 77, which in our view falls outside the scope of this political declaration and in our view does not contribute directly to the agreed objective of ending AIDS as a public health threat. Furthermore, references to legal and policy reforms, key populations, comprehensive sexuality education, sexual and reproductive health and reproductive rights, rights and related terminology must be understood in accordance with national laws, national priorities, cultural values, and religious beliefs. Nothing in this Declaration should be interpreted as creating new rights or new international obligations. Mr. President, the success of this Declaration will ultimately be measured not by the breadth of concepts it contains, but by its tangible contribution to reducing new HIV infections, preventing AIDS-related death, health and strengthening national capacities to respond effectively to the epidemic. The United Republic of Tanzania remains firmly committed to the global goal of ending AIDS as a public health threat. While maintaining reservations on specific provisions, my delegation voted in favor of the declaration because the global goal of ending AIDS is much greater than our minor differences. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Republic of Tanzania. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia.

Thank you, Mr. President. At the outset, Indonesia expresses its appreciation to Georgia and Botswana for their tireless efforts in facilitating the negotiations that led to the adoption of the political declaration today. Indonesia affirms that every human being has the right without discrimination to enjoy the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health. This commitment is reflected in our national laws and policies, as well as in our continued efforts to strengthen primary healthcare systems to ensure that HIV prevention, treatment, care, and support services are accessible, affordable, and responsive to the needs of our people. Indonesia also underscores the importance of ensuring equitable access to medicines, diagnostics, vaccines, and other health technologies to protect public health. It is on this basis that Indonesia supports the renewed global commitment to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030 and has voted in favor of the adoption of the political declaration. However, we regret that several sensitive and ambiguous terminologies which have been the subject of extensive discussions in previous negotiations have once again been retained in 2026 Political Declaration. Persistent inclusion of such language risks diverting the focus from our shared objective of accelerating action to end AIDS and may not contribute to the spirit of consensus that should guide multilateral negotiations. It is therefore Indonesia wishes to express its reservation for the terminologies that do not enjoy international consensus, including multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination, sexual and gender-based violence, where such terminology may be interpreted as extending beyond violence against women and girls, and language that may be interpreted as implying comprehensive sexuality education. Looking ahead, Indonesia remains committed committed to advancing comprehensive, people-centered, and nationally owned responses to HIV and AIDS at both the national and local levels in accordance with our national circumstances, development priorities, and international commitments. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Indonesia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malaysia.

Thank you, Mr. President. Malaysia voted in favour of the Political Declaration as it represents a collective commitment by the international community to accelerate efforts towards ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030. We commend the co-facilitators and all delegations for their efforts throughout the negotiation. While no outcome of this nature can fully reflect the positions of all member states, The Declaration provides a useful framework to strengthen prevention, treatment, care and support services, promote resilient health systems, and advance international cooperation in addressing the HIV/AIDS epidemic. Malaysia particularly welcomes the Declaration's recognition of the importance of sustainable financing and international cooperation, as many developing countries continue to face resource constraints and evolving public health challenges, predictable financing, strengthened health systems, capacity building, technology transfer, and affordable access to medicines and health technologies remain essential to sustaining progress towards the 2030 targets. At the same time, Malaysia wishes to place on record its understanding that certain terms and concepts referenced in the text including multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination, will be interpreted strictly in accordance with our national laws, values, and customs, and does not include any concepts that are inconsistent with the existing international human rights architecture. Malaysia further reiterates that the implementation of the Political Declaration will be undertaken in accordance with our national laws, national development priorities, and national strategy. Malaysia's support for the political declaration reflects our conviction that efforts to end AIDS as a public health threat must be guided by evidence, science, and public health considerations, including measures aimed at improving access to prevention, testing, treatment, and care services for, for those most vulnerable to HIV infection. It should not be construed as an endorsement of any to a particular lifestyle, behavior, or social construct. Mr. President, Malaysia remains committed to working constructively with Member States, UNAIDS, civil society, and all relevant stakeholders to accelerate progress towards ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2020. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malaysia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Canada.

Thank you, Excellencies. On behalf of Canada, I would like to thank our esteemed colleagues from Botswana and Georgia for their co-facilitation and steady leadership throughout this process. I also thank my colleague from Australia who has delivered our joint statement on behalf of CANZ, and I take the floor briefly to underscore a point of concern.
